q: Income rises for a normal good while the price of a close substitute falls. What can be concluded about demand for the normal good?
correctAnswer: The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.
distractors: Demand must rise because the income effect necessarily dominates the substitute effect.
Demand must fall because the substitute-price effect necessarily dominates the income effect.
Only quantity demanded changes because neither event can shift the demand curve.
commonError: Assuming one of two opposing demand shifters must dominate.
feedback: Higher income raises demand for a normal good, while a cheaper substitute lowers it. The net shift depends on the relative size of the effects.
options: The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.
Demand must rise because the income effect necessarily dominates the substitute effect.
Demand must fall because the substitute-price effect necessarily dominates the income effect.
Only quantity demanded changes because neither event can shift the demand curve.

q: A survey shows buyers want more electric scooters at every listed price than they did last month. Which statement is most precise?
correctAnswer: Demand increased, so the entire demand schedule shifted right.
distractors: Quantity demanded increased because the scooter price fell.
Demand increased only at the market price.
The law of demand stopped applying to electric scooters.
commonError: Calling an across-the-board schedule change a movement along demand.
feedback: Wanting more at every price is a rightward shift of demand, not a change in quantity demanded caused by the good’s own price.
options: Quantity demanded increased because the scooter price fell.
Demand increased, so the entire demand schedule shifted right.
Demand increased only at the market price.
The law of demand stopped applying to electric scooters.

q: Coffee is a normal good. Consumer income rises, buyers expect coffee prices to fall next month, and the current price of tea, a substitute, rises. What can be concluded about current coffee demand?
correctAnswer: The direction is ambiguous because two forces raise current demand while one lowers it.
distractors: Current demand must rise because income and tea prices both increased.
Current demand must fall because buyers expect a lower future coffee price.
Current quantity demanded changes, but the demand curve cannot shift.
commonError: Adding demand shifters mechanically without recognizing opposing effects.
feedback: Higher income and a higher substitute price raise current coffee demand, while expecting a lower future coffee price reduces current demand. Magnitudes determine the net shift.
options: Current demand must rise because income and tea prices both increased.
Current demand must fall because buyers expect a lower future coffee price.
The direction is ambiguous because two forces raise current demand while one lowers it.
Current quantity demanded changes, but the demand curve cannot shift.

q: The good’s own price declines while every non-price determinant stays fixed. Which demand-side change occurs?
correctAnswer: Quantity demanded increases through a movement along the existing curve.
distractors: Demand increases through a rightward shift of the curve.
Demand decreases through a leftward shift of the curve.
Quantity demanded stays fixed because the curve did not shift.
commonError: Using demand and quantity demanded as interchangeable terms.
feedback: A change in the good’s own price causes movement along the demand curve and changes quantity demanded.
options: Demand increases through a rightward shift of the curve.
Demand decreases through a leftward shift of the curve.
Quantity demanded stays fixed because the curve did not shift.
Quantity demanded increases through a movement along the existing curve.

q: Which event shifts demand for bus rides to the right?
correctAnswer: The price of subway rides, a substitute, increases.
distractors: The price of bus rides decreases while all non-price determinants remain fixed.
Bus companies add routes and lower their operating costs.
The cost of diesel fuel decreases for bus operators.
commonError: Selecting an own-price movement or a supply shifter as a demand shifter.
feedback: A higher price for a substitute makes bus rides more attractive at every bus fare and shifts demand right.
options: The price of subway rides, a substitute, increases.
The price of bus rides decreases while all non-price determinants remain fixed.
Bus companies add routes and lower their operating costs.
The cost of diesel fuel decreases for bus operators.

q: Income falls and purchases of instant noodles rise. What does this evidence suggest?
correctAnswer: Instant noodles are an inferior good for these consumers.
distractors: Instant noodles are a normal good for these consumers.
The price of instant noodles must have increased.
The supply of instant noodles must have decreased.
commonError: Treating all goods as normal or confusing demand evidence with supply.
feedback: Demand for an inferior good rises when income falls, holding other determinants constant.
options: Instant noodles are a normal good for these consumers.
Instant noodles are an inferior good for these consumers.
The price of instant noodles must have increased.
The supply of instant noodles must have decreased.

q: A product’s price is unchanged, yet buyers plan to purchase less at every possible price. Which explanation is consistent with the evidence?
correctAnswer: A non-price determinant reduced demand and shifted the curve left.
distractors: The product’s own price caused a movement up the demand curve.
Supply increased and forced buyers to reduce demand.
Quantity demanded fell while the demand schedule stayed unchanged.
commonError: Explaining a full demand-schedule change as movement along one curve.
feedback: Less desired at every price means demand shifted left because a non-price determinant changed.
options: The product’s own price caused a movement up the demand curve.
Supply increased and forced buyers to reduce demand.
A non-price determinant reduced demand and shifted the curve left.
Quantity demanded fell while the demand schedule stayed unchanged.

q: Movie tickets are a normal good. Income rises, but the price of streaming subscriptions, a substitute, falls. What is the strongest conclusion about movie-ticket demand?
correctAnswer: The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.
distractors: Demand must rise because the positive income effect always dominates related-good prices.
Demand must fall because the cheaper substitute always dominates changes in income.
Only quantity demanded changes because neither event can shift demand.
commonError: Claiming certainty when opposing demand shifters act simultaneously.
feedback: Higher income raises demand for a normal good, while a cheaper substitute lowers it. Effect sizes are required.
options: Demand must rise because the positive income effect always dominates related-good prices.
Demand must fall because the cheaper substitute always dominates changes in income.
Only quantity demanded changes because neither event can shift demand.
The net shift is uncertain because the two effects oppose each other.

q: The current price of concert tickets rises, attendance falls, and no other determinant changes. Which statement avoids the common terminology error?
correctAnswer: Quantity demanded fell; demand itself did not shift.
distractors: Demand fell because the ticket price increased.
Demand shifted left because attendance decreased.
Supply shifted right because fewer tickets were purchased.
commonError: Calling an own-price movement a change in demand.
feedback: An own-price change moves buyers along the existing demand curve and changes quantity demanded.
options: Quantity demanded fell; demand itself did not shift.
Demand fell because the ticket price increased.
Demand shifted left because attendance decreased.
Supply shifted right because fewer tickets were purchased.

q: Consumer confidence falls while a major productivity improvement lowers firms’ production costs. Without knowing the size of either shock, what is certain in the short run?
correctAnswer: The price level falls, while the change in real output remains uncertain.
distractors: Real output falls, while the price-level effect remains uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise because both shocks are expansionary.
Both real output and the price level fall because both shocks are contractionary.
commonError: Treating a negative demand shock and positive supply shock as if they move both outcomes in the same direction.
feedback: Lower aggregate demand and higher short-run aggregate supply both reduce the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.
options: Real output falls, while the price-level effect remains uncertain.
The price level falls, while the change in real output remains uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise because both shocks are expansionary.
Both real output and the price level fall because both shocks are contractionary.

q: An economy experiences an adverse supply shock. Policymakers fully stabilize real output with expansionary demand policy. What tradeoff follows?
correctAnswer: Output is stabilized, but inflation pressure becomes stronger.
distractors: The price level returns to its original value once output is restored.
Inflation and unemployment both fall because the policy removes the supply shock.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because aggregate demand rises.
commonError: Assuming demand policy can reverse a supply shock without an inflation cost.
feedback: Expansionary demand policy can offset the output loss from an adverse supply shock, but it intensifies inflation pressure.
options: The price level returns to its original value once output is restored.
Inflation and unemployment both fall because the policy removes the supply shock.
Output is stabilized, but inflation pressure becomes stronger.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because aggregate demand rises.

q: Real output rises while the price level falls. Which pair of simultaneous shifts can produce that pattern?
correctAnswer: Both curves shift right, with the supply shift dominating the price effect.
distractors: Both curves shift left, with the demand shift dominating the output effect.
Demand shifts right while supply shifts left, with demand dominating output.
Demand shifts left while supply shifts right, with demand dominating output.
commonError: Matching one observed outcome to one curve while ignoring the second observed outcome.
feedback: Higher output can come from either shift, but a falling price level requires the rightward supply shift to dominate the demand effect.
options: Both curves shift left, with the demand shift dominating the output effect.
Demand shifts right while supply shifts left, with demand dominating output.
Demand shifts left while supply shifts right, with demand dominating output.
Both curves shift right, with the supply shift dominating the price effect.

q: A sharp fall in household spending is primarily what kind of macroeconomic disturbance?
correctAnswer: A negative aggregate-demand shock.
distractors: A positive aggregate-demand shock.
A negative short-run aggregate-supply shock.
A positive short-run aggregate-supply shock.
commonError: Confusing a spending disturbance with a production-cost disturbance.
feedback: Household spending is a component of aggregate demand, so a sharp decline shifts aggregate demand left.
options: A negative aggregate-demand shock.
A positive aggregate-demand shock.
A negative short-run aggregate-supply shock.
A positive short-run aggregate-supply shock.

q: An unexpected increase in energy costs usually shifts which curve first?
correctAnswer: Short-run aggregate supply shifts left.
distractors: Aggregate demand shifts left.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts right immediately.
commonError: Treating a production-cost shock as a demand shock.
feedback: Higher energy costs raise firms’ costs and reduce output supplied at each price level, shifting short-run aggregate supply left.
options: Aggregate demand shifts left.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts left.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right.
Long-run aggregate supply shifts right immediately.

q: A negative aggregate-demand shock normally causes what short-run combination?
correctAnswer: Lower real output and a lower price level.
distractors: Lower real output and a higher price level.
Higher real output and a lower price level.
Higher real output and a higher price level.
commonError: Reversing the price-level effect of a demand contraction.
feedback: A leftward aggregate-demand shift reduces both equilibrium output and the price level in the short run.
options: Lower real output and a higher price level.
Higher real output and a lower price level.
Lower real output and a lower price level.
Higher real output and a higher price level.

q: A surge in business investment shifts aggregate demand right. In the short run, what happens other things equal?
correctAnswer: Real output and the price level both rise.
distractors: Real output rises and the price level falls.
Real output falls and the price level rises.
Real output and the price level both fall.
commonError: Using supply-shock outcomes for a demand expansion.
feedback: A rightward aggregate-demand shift moves the economy to higher short-run output and a higher price level.
options: Real output rises and the price level falls.
Real output falls and the price level rises.
Real output and the price level both fall.
Real output and the price level both rise.

q: A widespread crop failure raises food-production costs. Which short-run outcome is most likely?
correctAnswer: Real output falls while the price level rises.
distractors: Real output rises while the price level falls.
Real output and the price level both rise.
Real output and the price level both fall.
commonError: Forgetting that an adverse supply shock creates stagflation pressure.
feedback: An adverse supply shock shifts short-run aggregate supply left, lowering output and raising the price level.
options: Real output falls while the price level rises.
Real output rises while the price level falls.
Real output and the price level both rise.
Real output and the price level both fall.

q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply is unchanged. Which policy direction would most directly offset the output loss?
correctAnswer: Expansionary demand policy.
distractors: Contractionary demand policy.
A policy that shifts aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect aggregate demand.
commonError: Choosing contractionary policy during a demand-driven recession.
feedback: Expansionary fiscal or monetary policy can shift aggregate demand right and counter a negative demand shock.
options: Contractionary demand policy.
Expansionary demand policy.
A policy that shifts aggregate supply left.
No policy can affect aggregate demand.

q: Aggregate demand rises while short-run aggregate supply falls. What can be predicted with certainty?
correctAnswer: The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
distractors: Real output rises, while the price level is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output rises.
Both the price level and real output fall.
commonError: Claiming certainty about output when the two shocks move output in opposite directions.
feedback: Both shifts raise the price level, but aggregate demand raises output while adverse supply lowers it.
options: Real output rises, while the price level is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output rises.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
Both the price level and real output fall.

q: Aggregate demand falls while short-run aggregate supply rises. Which outcome is certain?
correctAnswer: The price level falls, while real output is uncertain.
distractors: Real output falls, while the price level is uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
commonError: Missing the shared price-level direction of the two shifts.
feedback: A demand contraction and favorable supply shock both lower the price level, but they push output in opposite directions.
options: Real output falls, while the price level is uncertain.
Both real output and the price level rise.
The price level rises, while real output is uncertain.
The price level falls, while real output is uncertain.

q: After an adverse supply shock, policymakers use expansionary demand policy to restore output. Which risk remains?
correctAnswer: The price level may rise even more than it did from the original shock.
distractors: Unemployment must rise because aggregate demand increased.
Short-run aggregate supply automatically returns to its old position.
The economy must move below potential output.
commonError: Assuming output stabilization eliminates the inflation tradeoff.
feedback: Demand expansion can support output after a supply shock, but it adds inflation pressure rather than repairing supply.
options: The price level may rise even more than it did from the original shock.
Unemployment must rise because aggregate demand increased.
Short-run aggregate supply automatically returns to its old position.
The economy must move below potential output.

q: Government purchases rise while a technology breakthrough lowers unit costs. If output rises but the price level is unchanged, what does the evidence imply?
correctAnswer: The opposing price effects approximately offset while both shifts raise output.
distractors: Neither curve shifted because the price level did not change.
Aggregate demand fell while short-run aggregate supply rose.
Aggregate demand rose while short-run aggregate supply fell.
commonError: Assuming an unchanged price level means no macroeconomic shifts occurred.
feedback: Higher government purchases shift aggregate demand right and better technology shifts short-run aggregate supply right. Both raise output, while their price effects can offset.
options: Neither curve shifted because the price level did not change.
The opposing price effects approximately offset while both shifts raise output.
Aggregate demand fell while short-run aggregate supply rose.
Aggregate demand rose while short-run aggregate supply fell.

q: Oil prices rise sharply and the central bank expands aggregate demand enough to keep real output unchanged. Compared with the initial equilibrium, what is most likely?
correctAnswer: The price level is higher because both the supply shock and policy raise it.
distractors: The price level is unchanged because real output is unchanged.
The price level is lower because monetary expansion reduces costs.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because interest rates fall.
commonError: Equating stable output with a stable price level.
feedback: The adverse supply shock raises the price level, and the demand expansion used to stabilize output adds additional price pressure.
options: The price level is unchanged because real output is unchanged.
The price level is lower because monetary expansion reduces costs.
The price level is higher because both the supply shock and policy raise it.
Short-run aggregate supply shifts right because interest rates fall.

q: Consumer spending collapses at the same time firms adopt a major cost-saving technology. Prices fall sharply, but output changes little. Which interpretation fits best?
correctAnswer: A negative demand shock and positive supply shock had offsetting output effects.
distractors: A positive demand shock and adverse supply shock offset in the price level.
Only aggregate demand shifted because prices fell.
Only short-run aggregate supply shifted because output was stable.
commonError: Using one observed variable to infer only one curve shifted.
feedback: Both shocks lower the price level, while one lowers output and the other raises it. Similar magnitudes can leave output nearly unchanged.
options: A positive demand shock and adverse supply shock offset in the price level.
Only aggregate demand shifted because prices fell.
Only short-run aggregate supply shifted because output was stable.
A negative demand shock and positive supply shock had offsetting output effects.

q: A household moves $4,000 from a checking account into a retail money-market mutual fund. Under standard textbook definitions, what happens?
correctAnswer: M1 falls while M2 is unchanged.
distractors: M1 and M2 both fall by $4,000.
M1 is unchanged while M2 rises.
M1 and M2 both rise by $4,000.
commonError: Treating movement between M1 and non-M1 M2 assets as a change in total M2.
feedback: Checking deposits are in M1 and M2, while retail money-market mutual funds are in M2 but not M1. The transfer lowers M1 without changing M2.
options: M1 falls while M2 is unchanged.
M1 and M2 both fall by $4,000.
M1 is unchanged while M2 rises.
M1 and M2 both rise by $4,000.

q: Which asset is included in M2 but normally excluded from M1?
correctAnswer: A small-denomination time deposit.
distractors: Currency held by the public.
Funds in a checking account.
Traveler’s checks held by households.
commonError: Placing every liquid financial asset in M1.
feedback: Small time deposits are near-money assets included in M2 but not in the narrower M1 measure.
options: Currency held by the public.
A small-denomination time deposit.
Funds in a checking account.
Traveler’s checks held by households.

q: A payment app transfers balances instantly from users’ checking accounts but holds no separate monetary balance. How should the app affect measured money?
correctAnswer: It changes payment convenience without creating a new money balance.
distractors: Every transfer through the app permanently increases the measured M1 stock.
The app balance enters M2 even though no separate monetary balance exists.
Using the app removes the linked checking deposits from measured money.
commonError: Counting a payment method as a separate stock of money when it only accesses an existing deposit.
feedback: A payment platform that merely accesses checking deposits changes how money is used, not how much money exists.
options: Every transfer through the app permanently increases the measured M1 stock.
The app balance enters M2 even though no separate monetary balance exists.
It changes payment convenience without creating a new money balance.
Using the app removes the linked checking deposits from measured money.

q: A store lists prices in dollars, accepts dollars at checkout, and households keep dollars for future purchases. Which statement is correct?
correctAnswer: Money is serving as unit of account, medium of exchange, and store of value.
distractors: Money is serving only as a medium of exchange during the checkout transaction.
Money is serving as a unit of account and barter device, but not as stored value.
Money is serving only as a store of value because households retain some dollars.
commonError: Assuming one transaction can illustrate only one function of money.
feedback: Money can perform all three functions in the same setting: quoting prices, settling purchases, and carrying purchasing power forward.
options: Money is serving only as a medium of exchange during the checkout transaction.
Money is serving as a unit of account and barter device, but not as stored value.
Money is serving only as a store of value because households retain some dollars.
Money is serving as unit of account, medium of exchange, and store of value.

q: Inflation accelerates, but dollars remain widely accepted and prices continue to be quoted in dollars. Which money function is most directly weakened?
correctAnswer: Store of value, because purchasing power erodes more quickly.
distractors: Medium of exchange, because dollars can no longer buy anything.
Unit of account, because prices cannot be stated in dollars.
Standard of deferred payment, because all credit disappears.
commonError: Assuming inflation eliminates every function of money equally.
feedback: Rapid inflation most directly weakens money’s ability to preserve purchasing power over time.
options: Store of value, because purchasing power erodes more quickly.
Medium of exchange, because dollars can no longer buy anything.
Unit of account, because prices cannot be stated in dollars.
Standard of deferred payment, because all credit disappears.

q: Currency held by the public rises by $20 billion, checking deposits fall by $20 billion, and small time deposits are unchanged. What happens to M1 and M2?
correctAnswer: Both aggregates are unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
distractors: M1 rises by $20 billion while M2 remains unchanged because currency is broader money.
M1 and M2 both fall by $20 billion because checking deposits decline.
M1 remains unchanged while M2 rises by $20 billion because currency increases.
commonError: Adding gross component changes without recognizing an offset within both aggregates.
feedback: Currency and checking deposits are both in M1 and M2. An equal transfer between them changes composition but not either total.
options: M1 rises by $20 billion while M2 remains unchanged because currency is broader money.
Both aggregates are unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
M1 and M2 both fall by $20 billion because checking deposits decline.
M1 remains unchanged while M2 rises by $20 billion because currency increases.

q: A new digital wallet stores claims on bank checking deposits and the same balances are still reported as checking deposits. How should statisticians avoid double counting?
correctAnswer: Count the underlying deposit once and do not add the wallet claim again.
distractors: Count both the checking deposit and the wallet claim as separate M1 balances.
Exclude the checking deposit and count only the wallet claim as part of M2.
Remove both records because digitally accessed balances cannot qualify as money.
commonError: Counting two records of the same underlying monetary claim as two balances.
feedback: A wallet claim backed one-for-one by an already-counted checking deposit is another access channel, not a second stock of money.
options: Count both the checking deposit and the wallet claim as separate M1 balances.
Exclude the checking deposit and count only the wallet claim as part of M2.
Count the underlying deposit once and do not add the wallet claim again.
Remove both records because digitally accessed balances cannot qualify as money.

q: An economy replaces an unstable commodity money with fiat currency. Which condition is most important for the fiat currency to function well?
correctAnswer: Users must trust its acceptance and the institutions supporting its value.
distractors: The currency must possess substantial nonmonetary commodity value in every use.
Every note must remain redeemable for a fixed quantity of gold or silver.
The government must prohibit bank deposits and all competing payment methods.
commonError: Assuming fiat money requires intrinsic commodity value.
feedback: Fiat money works because of general acceptability, legal and institutional support, and confidence in its purchasing power.
options: The currency must possess substantial nonmonetary commodity value in every use.
Every note must remain redeemable for a fixed quantity of gold or silver.
The government must prohibit bank deposits and all competing payment methods.
Users must trust its acceptance and the institutions supporting its value.

q: Which item belongs in M1 under standard textbook definitions?
correctAnswer: A balance in a checking account.
distractors: A small time deposit.
A retail money-market mutual fund.
A long-term corporate bond.
commonError: Including broad near-money assets in the narrow M1 measure.
feedback: Checking deposits are immediately spendable and are included in M1.
options: A balance in a checking account.
A small time deposit.
A retail money-market mutual fund.
A long-term corporate bond.

q: A restaurant posts every menu price in dollars. Which function of money is being used?
correctAnswer: Unit of account.
distractors: Medium of exchange.
Store of value.
Commodity backing.
commonError: Confusing the act of quoting prices with settling a transaction.
feedback: Money serves as a unit of account when it provides the common measurement used to state prices.
options: Medium of exchange.
Unit of account.
Store of value.
Commodity backing.

q: A saver moves funds from checking to a small time deposit. Which result is correct?
correctAnswer: M1 decreases, but M2 does not change.
distractors: M1 and M2 both decrease.
M1 does not change, but M2 increases.
M1 and M2 both increase.
commonError: Treating an internal transfer within M2 as a change in M2.
feedback: Checking is in M1 and M2; a small time deposit is in M2 only. The transfer lowers M1 but leaves M2 unchanged.
options: M1 and M2 both decrease.
M1 does not change, but M2 increases.
M1 decreases, but M2 does not change.
M1 and M2 both increase.

q: A bank customer withdraws $500 from checking and holds the cash. What happens to M1?
correctAnswer: M1 is unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.
distractors: M1 falls by $500 because checking deposits decline.
M1 rises by $500 because currency increases.
M1 falls while M2 rises by $500.
commonError: Looking at one component change without accounting for the offsetting M1 component.
feedback: Currency held by the public and checking deposits are both in M1, so the transfer changes composition rather than the total.
options: M1 falls by $500 because checking deposits decline.
M1 rises by $500 because currency increases.
M1 falls while M2 rises by $500.
M1 is unchanged because one M1 component replaces another.

q: An online service lets users pay merchants directly from savings accounts. What is the safest conclusion about money measurement?
correctAnswer: Classification still depends on the official definition of the account.
distractors: Every savings balance automatically moves into M1 once direct payments are possible.
The payment service creates new money each time a customer completes a purchase.
Savings accounts must be removed from M2 because they are now easier to spend.
commonError: Assuming technology alone automatically changes official monetary definitions.
feedback: A new payment channel can make an asset more usable without automatically changing how statistical agencies classify the underlying account.
options: Classification still depends on the official definition of the account.
Every savings balance automatically moves into M1 once direct payments are possible.
The payment service creates new money each time a customer completes a purchase.
Savings accounts must be removed from M2 because they are now easier to spend.

q: Prices are quoted in dollars, workers accept dollars as wages, and households save dollars for emergencies. What does this example show?
correctAnswer: Money is performing all three primary functions.
distractors: Money is performing only as a medium of exchange.
Money is performing only as a unit of account.
Money is performing only as a store of value.
commonError: Selecting one function when the scenario demonstrates several.
feedback: The dollar measures value, settles transactions, and transfers purchasing power over time.
options: Money is performing only as a medium of exchange.
Money is performing all three primary functions.
Money is performing only as a unit of account.
Money is performing only as a store of value.

q: M1 equals $900 billion and M2 equals $3.4 trillion. Households transfer $80 billion from checking deposits to small time deposits. What are the new values?
correctAnswer: M1 is $820 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
distractors: M1 remains $900 billion and M2 becomes $3.48 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 is $3.32 trillion.
M1 becomes $980 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
commonError: Subtracting the transfer from both aggregates instead of recognizing it remains inside M2.
feedback: The transfer leaves the broad M2 total unchanged but removes $80 billion from the narrower M1 measure.
options: M1 remains $900 billion and M2 becomes $3.48 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 is $3.32 trillion.
M1 is $820 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.
M1 becomes $980 billion and M2 remains $3.4 trillion.

q: A wallet provider reports $10 billion of customer balances that are fully backed by $10 billion already counted in bank checking deposits. What is the correct measurement treatment?
correctAnswer: Do not add the wallet balance unless it is a separate monetary liability.
distractors: Add the full wallet balance to both M1 and M2 even though the deposit is counted.
Remove the bank deposit and count only the wallet balance in the money stock.
Exclude both balances because electronic monetary claims cannot be measured.
commonError: Double counting an access claim and the underlying deposit.
feedback: If the wallet balance is simply a claim on an already-counted deposit, adding both would overstate the money stock.
options: Add the full wallet balance to both M1 and M2 even though the deposit is counted.
Remove the bank deposit and count only the wallet balance in the money stock.
Exclude both balances because electronic monetary claims cannot be measured.
Do not add the wallet balance unless it is a separate monetary liability.

q: The central bank raises the interest rate paid on reserve balances. What response is most likely, other things equal?
correctAnswer: Banks are more willing to hold reserves and less willing to expand lending.
distractors: Banks reduce reserve holdings and expand lending because reserves now pay more.
Households move currency directly into government spending when reserves earn more.
The required reserve ratio automatically falls when reserve interest increases.
commonError: Reversing the incentive effect of higher interest paid on reserves.
feedback: A higher return on reserve balances makes reserve holding more attractive and tends to restrain lending and money creation.
options: Banks are more willing to hold reserves and less willing to expand lending.
Banks reduce reserve holdings and expand lending because reserves now pay more.
Households move currency directly into government spending when reserves earn more.
The required reserve ratio automatically falls when reserve interest increases.

q: To increase banking-system reserves through open-market operations, the central bank should:
correctAnswer: Buy government securities.
distractors: Sell government securities.
Raise taxes.
Increase reserve requirements.
commonError: Reversing the reserve effect of an open-market purchase.
feedback: When the central bank buys securities, it pays by adding reserves to the banking system.
options: Sell government securities.
Buy government securities.
Raise taxes.
Increase reserve requirements.

q: What is the usual effect of lowering the discount rate?
correctAnswer: Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks.
distractors: Banks must hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves.
The central bank removes reserves by selling bonds.
Households are required to reduce currency holdings.
commonError: Confusing the discount rate with reserve requirements or open-market sales.
feedback: A lower discount rate reduces the cost of borrowing reserves directly from the central bank.
options: Banks must hold a larger fraction of deposits as reserves.
The central bank removes reserves by selling bonds.
Borrowing from the central bank becomes less costly for banks.
Households are required to reduce currency holdings.

q: Which policy action is contractionary?
correctAnswer: Selling government securities in the open market.
distractors: Buying government securities in the open market.
Lowering the interest paid on reserve balances.
Lowering reserve requirements.
commonError: Selecting an expansionary tool as contractionary.
feedback: An open-market sale withdraws reserves and tends to reduce money and credit expansion.
options: Buying government securities in the open market.
Lowering the interest paid on reserve balances.
Lowering reserve requirements.
Selling government securities in the open market.

q: The central bank buys securities but simultaneously raises the interest paid on reserves. Why might lending rise by less than expected?
correctAnswer: The purchase adds reserves, but the higher reserve return encourages banks to hold them.
distractors: Both actions remove reserves and directly reduce the banking system’s lending capacity.
The bond purchase automatically raises reserve requirements and blocks new loans.
The higher reserve return forces banks to lend every newly created reserve dollar.
commonError: Assuming every tool in a policy package pushes bank lending in the same direction.
feedback: The open-market purchase is expansionary, while a higher return on reserves can weaken the lending response.
options: The purchase adds reserves, but the higher reserve return encourages banks to hold them.
Both actions remove reserves and directly reduce the banking system’s lending capacity.
The bond purchase automatically raises reserve requirements and blocks new loans.
The higher reserve return forces banks to lend every newly created reserve dollar.

q: A central bank wants to drain reserves quickly without changing reserve requirements. Which action is most direct?
correctAnswer: Sell government securities and debit reserve accounts.
distractors: Buy government securities and credit reserve accounts.
Lower the discount rate to make reserve borrowing cheaper.
Lower interest paid on reserves to discourage reserve holding.
commonError: Choosing an expansionary action when the goal is to remove reserves.
feedback: An open-market sale receives payment from the banking system and reduces reserves directly.
options: Buy government securities and credit reserve accounts.
Sell government securities and debit reserve accounts.
Lower the discount rate to make reserve borrowing cheaper.
Lower interest paid on reserves to discourage reserve holding.

q: Reserve requirements are lowered, but banks expect severe loan losses and keep the newly available reserves idle. What does this illustrate?
correctAnswer: Policy can expand lending capacity without guaranteeing that banks will lend.
distractors: Lower reserve requirements always produce the full textbook deposit multiplier.
Banks lose the legal ability to hold excess reserves after requirements decline.
The central bank shifts aggregate supply left whenever it changes reserve rules.
commonError: Treating potential money creation as automatic actual money creation.
feedback: Lower reserve requirements free reserves for lending, but risk perceptions and bank choices can weaken the actual expansion.
options: Lower reserve requirements always produce the full textbook deposit multiplier.
Banks lose the legal ability to hold excess reserves after requirements decline.
Policy can expand lending capacity without guaranteeing that banks will lend.
The central bank shifts aggregate supply left whenever it changes reserve rules.

q: Real income rises and the central bank increases the money supply enough to leave the equilibrium interest rate unchanged. What must be true?
correctAnswer: The money-supply increase offset the rise in money demand.
distractors: Money demand stayed fixed even though higher income increased transaction volume.
The money supply shifted left by enough to offset the rise in money demand.
The price level fell to zero and eliminated the need to hold transaction balances.
commonError: Assuming an unchanged interest rate means neither curve shifted.
feedback: Higher income raises money demand. A sufficiently large increase in money supply can offset that pressure and leave the equilibrium interest rate unchanged.
options: Money demand stayed fixed even though higher income increased transaction volume.
The money supply shifted left by enough to offset the rise in money demand.
The price level fell to zero and eliminated the need to hold transaction balances.
The money-supply increase offset the rise in money demand.

q: In the liquidity-preference model, the opportunity cost of holding money is the:
correctAnswer: Interest income forgone by not holding interest-bearing assets.
distractors: The current price level paid for goods and services during the year.
The required reserve ratio applied to deposits held by commercial banks.
The previous year’s inflation rate reported by the statistical agency.
commonError: Confusing the opportunity cost of money with a price index or reserve rule.
feedback: Holding money sacrifices the interest that could have been earned on bonds or other interest-bearing assets.
options: Interest income forgone by not holding interest-bearing assets.
The current price level paid for goods and services during the year.
The required reserve ratio applied to deposits held by commercial banks.
The previous year’s inflation rate reported by the statistical agency.

q: If the money supply increases while money demand is unchanged, the equilibrium interest rate tends to:
correctAnswer: Fall.
distractors: Rise.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to the inflation rate.
commonError: Reversing the interest-rate effect of a rightward money-supply shift.
feedback: More money supplied at each interest rate creates excess money balances until the interest rate falls.
options: Rise.
Fall.
Remain fixed by definition.
Become equal to the inflation rate.

q: Which event shifts money demand to the right?
correctAnswer: An increase in real income and transactions.
distractors: An open-market purchase that increases money supply.
A decrease in the amount of currency printed.
A lower required reserve ratio by itself.
commonError: Selecting a money-supply event as a money-demand shifter.
feedback: Higher income generates more transactions and raises the quantity of money people want to hold at each interest rate.
options: An open-market purchase that increases money supply.
A decrease in the amount of currency printed.
An increase in real income and transactions.
A lower required reserve ratio by itself.

q: The price level rises while the nominal money supply is fixed. What happens in the money market?
correctAnswer: Money demand rises and the equilibrium interest rate increases.
distractors: Money demand falls and the equilibrium interest rate decreases.
Money supply rises and the equilibrium interest rate decreases.
Both curves remain fixed because only prices changed.
commonError: Ignoring the transaction-money demand created by a higher price level.
feedback: A higher price level increases nominal transaction needs, shifting money demand right and raising the interest rate with fixed supply.
options: Money demand falls and the equilibrium interest rate decreases.
Money supply rises and the equilibrium interest rate decreases.
Both curves remain fixed because only prices changed.
Money demand rises and the equilibrium interest rate increases.

q: The central bank increases the money supply. Through the interest-rate effect, what happens next?
correctAnswer: The interest rate falls, encouraging investment and aggregate demand.
distractors: The interest rate rises, reducing investment and aggregate demand.
The price level falls before the interest rate changes.
Money demand shifts left because reserves increased.
commonError: Reversing the monetary-policy transmission chain.
feedback: A larger money supply lowers the equilibrium interest rate, which tends to increase interest-sensitive spending.
options: The interest rate falls, encouraging investment and aggregate demand.
The interest rate rises, reducing investment and aggregate demand.
The price level falls before the interest rate changes.
Money demand shifts left because reserves increased.

q: Real income falls while the money supply is fixed. What is the likely equilibrium change?
correctAnswer: Money demand falls and the interest rate decreases.
distractors: Money demand rises and the interest rate increases.
Money supply falls and the interest rate increases.
Money demand is unchanged because income is real.
commonError: Reversing the money-demand response to lower transaction volume.
feedback: Lower real income reduces transactions, shifts money demand left, and lowers the equilibrium interest rate.
options: Money demand rises and the interest rate increases.
Money demand falls and the interest rate decreases.
Money supply falls and the interest rate increases.
Money demand is unchanged because income is real.

q: The price level rises and shifts money demand right. The central bank wants to keep the interest rate unchanged. What action fits the model?
correctAnswer: Increase the money supply enough to match the higher money demand.
distractors: Decrease the money supply by selling securities.
Hold money supply fixed and require less investment.
Shift aggregate supply left to reduce money demand.
commonError: Using contractionary policy to offset a rightward money-demand shift.
feedback: To prevent the interest rate from rising when money demand shifts right, the central bank must shift money supply right as well.
options: Decrease the money supply by selling securities.
Hold money supply fixed and require less investment.
Increase the money supply enough to match the higher money demand.
Shift aggregate supply left to reduce money demand.

q: Which transaction is included in current-year GDP?
correctAnswer: A newly produced refrigerator purchased by a household.
distractors: A used refrigerator resold by its owner.
A household purchase of corporate stock.
An unpaid repair performed by the homeowner.
commonError: Counting asset transfers, used goods, or unpaid household work as current production.
feedback: GDP includes newly produced final goods and services, not transfers of existing assets or unpaid household production.
options: A used refrigerator resold by its owner.
A household purchase of corporate stock.
An unpaid repair performed by the homeowner.
A newly produced refrigerator purchased by a household.

q: A bakery buys flour for $2 and sells bread to a household for $5. How much does the bread transaction add to GDP if the flour was produced this year?
correctAnswer: $5, because the final sale already includes the flour’s value.
distractors: $7, because both the flour and bread sales are added.
$3, because only the bakery’s value added counts and the flour is excluded everywhere.
$2, because intermediate goods are the only production counted.
commonError: Double counting an intermediate input and the final product.
feedback: Counting the $5 final bread sale captures the value of the flour and the bakery’s value added without double counting.
options: $5, because the final sale already includes the flour’s value.
$7, because both the flour and bread sales are added.
$3, because only the bakery’s value added counts and the flour is excluded everywhere.
$2, because intermediate goods are the only production counted.

q: Why does total income equal total expenditure in the national accounts?
correctAnswer: Each transaction is spending for a buyer and income for a seller.
distractors: Government legally requires national income to equal national expenditure each year.
Households always spend every dollar of income and never save financial assets.
Imports are recorded as both domestic production income and domestic expenditure.
commonError: Treating the accounting identity as a behavioral claim that everyone spends all income.
feedback: The same transaction is recorded from two sides: one party’s expenditure is another party’s income.
options: Government legally requires national income to equal national expenditure each year.
Each transaction is spending for a buyer and income for a seller.
Households always spend every dollar of income and never save financial assets.
Imports are recorded as both domestic production income and domestic expenditure.

q: A domestic firm produces a machine this year but does not sell it until next year. How is the machine treated this year?
correctAnswer: It is counted as inventory investment in this year’s GDP.
distractors: It is excluded until a customer buys it next year.
It is counted as household consumption this year.
It is counted only if the firm imports the parts.
commonError: Assuming unsold output is not counted until the final sale.
feedback: Newly produced unsold goods enter inventories, which are counted as investment in the year of production.
options: It is excluded until a customer buys it next year.
It is counted as household consumption this year.
It is counted as inventory investment in this year’s GDP.
It is counted only if the firm imports the parts.

q: A U.S.-owned factory located in Mexico produces a car. Which statement is correct for U.S. GDP?
correctAnswer: The car is excluded because it was produced outside the United States.
distractors: The car is included because the factory has a U.S. owner.
The car is included only if sold to a U.S. resident.
The car is counted as U.S. government production.
commonError: Using ownership instead of location to define domestic product.
feedback: GDP is based on production within a country’s borders, regardless of the producer’s nationality.
options: The car is included because the factory has a U.S. owner.
The car is included only if sold to a U.S. resident.
The car is counted as U.S. government production.
The car is excluded because it was produced outside the United States.

q: A homeowner buys paint for $200 and paints the house without pay. What enters GDP?
correctAnswer: The $200 market purchase of paint, but not the unpaid painting service.
distractors: Both the paint and an imputed value for the homeowner’s labor.
Only the homeowner’s labor because it creates the final service.
Neither the paint nor the labor because the house already existed.
commonError: Excluding a purchased input because the final service is unpaid, or imputing all household labor.
feedback: The market purchase of paint is counted, while unpaid household labor generally is not recorded in GDP.
options: The $200 market purchase of paint, but not the unpaid painting service.
Both the paint and an imputed value for the homeowner’s labor.
Only the homeowner’s labor because it creates the final service.
Neither the paint nor the labor because the house already existed.

q: At the equilibrium price, quantity demanded is:
correctAnswer: Equal to quantity supplied.
distractors: Greater than quantity supplied.
Less than quantity supplied.
Unrelated to quantity supplied.
commonError: Defining equilibrium as a shortage, surplus, or unrelated quantities.
feedback: Market equilibrium occurs at the price where buyers’ quantity demanded equals sellers’ quantity supplied.
options: Greater than quantity supplied.
Equal to quantity supplied.
Less than quantity supplied.
Unrelated to quantity supplied.

q: Demand and supply both increase. The equilibrium quantity rises, but the equilibrium price is unchanged. What does this reveal?
correctAnswer: The price effects offset, while both shifts raise equilibrium quantity.
distractors: Neither curve shifted because an unchanged price proves the market did not move.
Demand increased more than supply, so price should have risen instead of staying fixed.
Supply decreased while demand increased, creating offsetting quantity effects.
commonError: Assuming an unchanged price means the market experienced no shifts.
feedback: A demand increase raises price and quantity, while a supply increase lowers price and raises quantity. Equal price effects can cancel while quantity rises.
options: Neither curve shifted because an unchanged price proves the market did not move.
Demand increased more than supply, so price should have risen instead of staying fixed.
The price effects offset, while both shifts raise equilibrium quantity.
Supply decreased while demand increased, creating offsetting quantity effects.

q: A market price below equilibrium creates a:
correctAnswer: Shortage.
distractors: Surplus.
Balanced market.
Leftward demand shift.
commonError: Reversing shortage and surplus conditions.
feedback: Below equilibrium, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied, creating a shortage.
options: Surplus.
Balanced market.
Leftward demand shift.
Shortage.

q: What pressure does a surplus create in an unregulated market?
correctAnswer: Sellers lower prices to clear unwanted inventories.
distractors: Buyers bid prices higher because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
Demand shifts right until buyers absorb every unit offered for sale.
Supply shifts left because firms are holding unwanted inventories.
commonError: Reversing the price adjustment associated with a surplus.
feedback: When quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, sellers compete to clear inventory by lowering price.
options: Sellers lower prices to clear unwanted inventories.
Buyers bid prices higher because quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied.
Demand shifts right until buyers absorb every unit offered for sale.
Supply shifts left because firms are holding unwanted inventories.

q: If demand increases while supply is unchanged, equilibrium price and quantity usually:
correctAnswer: Both increase.
distractors: Both decrease.
Price rises and quantity falls.
Price falls and quantity rises.
commonError: Using the supply-shift outcome for a demand increase.
feedback: A rightward demand shift moves the equilibrium up along the supply curve to a higher price and quantity.
options: Both decrease.
Both increase.
Price rises and quantity falls.
Price falls and quantity rises.

q: Demand increases while supply decreases. Which equilibrium outcome is certain?
correctAnswer: The equilibrium price rises.
distractors: The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
The equilibrium price falls.
commonError: Claiming certainty about quantity when the two shifts move quantity in opposite directions.
feedback: Both shifts raise price, while demand raises quantity and lower supply reduces quantity.
options: The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.
The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.

q: Both demand and supply shift left in the same market. Which equilibrium result can be stated without knowing the shift sizes?
correctAnswer: The equilibrium quantity falls.
distractors: The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
The equilibrium quantity rises.
commonError: Claiming certainty about price when both curves shift left.
feedback: Both shifts reduce equilibrium quantity, but their price effects oppose each other.
options: The equilibrium price rises.
The equilibrium price falls.
The equilibrium quantity rises.
The equilibrium quantity falls.

q: At the current price, quantity demanded is 400 and quantity supplied is 520. What adjustment is expected without a price control?
correctAnswer: A surplus pushes the price downward toward equilibrium.
distractors: A shortage pushes the price upward toward equilibrium.
Demand shifts right until the surplus disappears.
Supply shifts left immediately because inventories exist.
commonError: Treating a surplus as a shortage or confusing movement along curves with shifts.
feedback: Quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, so sellers lower price, increasing quantity demanded and reducing quantity supplied along the curves.
options: A surplus pushes the price downward toward equilibrium.
A shortage pushes the price upward toward equilibrium.
Demand shifts right until the surplus disappears.
Supply shifts left immediately because inventories exist.

q: At the current price, quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied. What market condition exists?
correctAnswer: A shortage exists because buyers want more than sellers offer.
distractors: A surplus exists because sellers offer more than buyers want.
The market is in equilibrium because both quantities are positive.
Demand must shift left before any price adjustment can occur.
commonError: Reversing shortage and surplus or treating disequilibrium as a curve shift.
feedback: When quantity demanded is greater than quantity supplied at the current price, the market has a shortage and upward price pressure.
options: A surplus exists because sellers offer more than buyers want.
A shortage exists because buyers want more than sellers offer.
The market is in equilibrium because both quantities are positive.
Demand must shift left before any price adjustment can occur.
